concerns.text: The validation design relies on a paired t-test comparing the ML model's MAE against a 'mean-baseline model's MAE' (FR-005, SC-002). This is a tautological validation. A mean-baseline model predicts the global average of the target variable ($T_g$) for every sample. By definition, any model with non-zero predictive power (R² > 0) will have a lower MAE than the mean-baseline. The statistical test will almost certainly yield p < 0.05 simply because the ML model uses features, not because the specific compositional descriptors are scientifically meaningful. This validates the trivial fact that 'features exist' rather than the hypothesis that 'composition determines Tg'.

The proposed statistical comparison (paired t-test on MAE between ML and mean-baseline) is methodologically unsound for establishing scientific significance in this context. The mean-baseline is a degenerate model with zero degrees of freedom regarding the input features. Comparing a complex model to a constant predictor does not test the 'predictive information content' of composition; it only tests if the variance in $T_g$ is non-zero. A valid scientific validation requires comparison against a physics-based heuristic (e.g., a linear mixing rule or a known structure-property model) or a null model that accounts for the specific distribution of the data, not just the global mean.

The spec requires validating feature importance via permutation importance (FR-006) but fails to address the high multicollinearity inherent in compositional data (sum-to-one constraint). In glass science, increasing the fraction of one oxide (e.g., SiO2) necessitates decreasing others. Permutation importance on highly correlated features often yields unstable or misleading rankings because shuffling one feature breaks the physical constraint of the composition, creating 'impossible' glass samples that the model has never seen. The methodology does not account for this domain-specific data structure, risking invalid scientific conclusions about 'key drivers'.
